query: How can we formally model spatial interference—exposure mappings by distance bands, partial-interference blocks, or network-contagion models—and which approaches yield identifiable spillover estimates?

response.query: How can we formally model spatial interference—exposure mappings by distance bands, partial-interference blocks, or network-contagion models—and which approaches yield identifiable spillover estimates?
response.answer: Spatial interference can be modeled using generalized propensity score methods and network-based causal inference frameworks to yield identifiable spillover estimates. Bayesian nonparametric models and Markovian interference approaches also provide effective frameworks for this purpose.

results.title: Generalized propensity score approach to causal inference with spatial interference - PMC
results.content: # Generalized propensity score approach to causal inference with spatial interference. We propose a new causal framework to recover direct and spill-over effects in the presence of spatial interference, taking into account that exposures at nearby locations are more influential than exposures at locations further apart. (2018) use a generalized propensity score method to estimate the effect of individual exposures, as well as the effects from “neighborhood” interference-that is, interference effects from subjects connected on the prespecified graph. In a setting without interference, and thus only direct exposure effects, the standard propensity score for binary exposures is defined as . In addition to the proposed generalized propensity score model, we estimate three comparison models: (i) the oracle model, , is the true model that includes otherwise unknown as a covariate, (ii) the local only model, , conditions on local covariates using splines, and (iii) the naive model, , simply regresses the outcome onto the exposures, but does not incorporate any causal conditioning. The generalized propensity score model performs substantially better than both the Local only and the Naive models, although, intuitively, the Local only model does show reasonable direct effect estimates. In addition to the generalized propensity score model, we estimate a model that conditions on the local covariates only, using splines. The causal direct effect estimate given by the generalized propensity score model is of , or 11.9% of the annual mean observed throughout. The generalized propensity score method presented here establishes a new framework to recover causal direct and spill-over effects in the presence of spatial interference, as well as estimate the range of the interference. We study nonparametric and regression estimators of treatment and spillover effects when interference is mediated by a network. Inference is nonstandard due to dependence induced by treatment spillovers and network-correlated effects. results.title: HETEROGENEOUS TREATMENT AND SPILLOVER EFFECTS UNDER CLUSTERED NETWORK INTERFERENCE - PMC
results.content: In this paper, we develop a machine learning method that uses tree-based algorithms and a Horvitz–Thompson estimator to assess the heterogeneity of treatment and spillover effects with respect to individual, neighborhood, and network characteristics in the context of clustered networks and interference within clusters. In this paper, we bridge the gap between the two strands of causal inference literature that focus on interference and heterogeneous causal effects1 by proposing a new algorithm for the interpretable discovery and estimation of heterogeneous treatment and spillover effects with respect to potentially a large number of characteristics, including individual and network features. Our proposed NCT differs from the standard causal tree algorithm in two critical aspects: (i) it detects and estimates heterogeneous causal effects—treatment and spillover effects—in the presence of clustered network interference, and (ii) it detects heterogeneity with respect to more than one effect at the same time through a composite splitting criterion. In particular, Section I.1 describes the results for a network exposure defined as having two or more treated friends, and Section I.2 presents the investigation of causal effects and their heterogeneities for the subset of households that received the information session at a delayed time with respect to the initial roll-out of the treatment. In this paper we have introduced a new algorithm to estimate heterogeneous causal treatment and spillover effects in the presence of clustered network interference. The main findings on average causal effects presented here, that is, a positive effect of directly receiving the intensive information session at round 1 and positive spillover effect in the subsample of households receiving the training at a delayed time, are consistent with those reported by Cai, De Janvry and Sadoulet (2015), despite the use of different estimators and different definitions of the network exposure mapping. Depending on the stopping rule, which might rely on the accuracy of the estimation of conditional effects or on the number of observations (see Section 5), if the sample size is not large enough with respect to the number of categories of the network exposure and/or its distribution is nonuniform and highly skewed, the network causal tree algorithm might result in a tree with low depth and low granularity, that is, with highly heterogeneous causal effects even within the terminal leaves.
